speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It would be negative of what is desired to be achieved. The first provision of this section is, "The provisions of this act shall bind His Majesty." The next is, "shall prevail over all inconsistent provisions of all other acts." That is, where there are provisions that are inconsistent, this act shall prevail over all inconsistent provisions of all other acts. As has been pointed out, it is desired to preserve three things, whether consistent or inconsistent with the provisions of this act. They are:
(a)	that part of section one hundred and seventy-nine of the Railway Act which relates to compensation of employees for financial loss caused to them by removal, closing or abandonment of any railway station or divisional point,
(b)	the provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act; and
(c)	the provisions of any statute of Canada which confirm any contract or enact or provide for any specific or special freight rate, toll or tariff or for the ascertainment of any one freight rate, toll or tariff by reference to any other and the making of deductions or allowances,
shall not be deemed to be inconsistent with the provisions of this act or to be in any manner affected thereby.
It will be observed that the section as amended would read:
The provisions of this act shall bind His Majesty and shall prevail when not inconsistent with the provisions of all other acts.
The rest of the section is struck out. There then would remain doubt as to the consistency or inconsistency of at least one of the three matters contained in the remainder of the section, The decision as to whether a provision is consistent or inconsistent is not quite as simple in a court of law as it seems to be in a committee of this house. This clause was framed with the idea of protecting beyond peradventure at least two of the three matters 
I have mentioned. The first is that of compensation to be paid to employees. It might well be that nothing in this act would be inconsistent with that provision, but in order that all doubt may be removed, it is specifically stated that this section is not intended to deprive any employee of compensation to which he may be entitled.

I find myself at variance with the opinion expressed by the Prime Minister. The difference between the amendment and the terms of the clause as it stands is this. Clause 2 as it now stands makes this act supreme over all inconsistent provisions of all other acts-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I am
coming to that, and then it specifically makes three exemptions referred to in (a), (b) and (c) of section 2. The intention, the purport and the effect of the amendment is to make this act prevail only where it is not inconsistent 53719-243 %
with other acts. In other words, there is not a single right that exists to-day in any other statute which is abrogated by this act, because it cannot prevail where it is inconsistent with the others. So that the effect of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Pro-vencher is to safeguard not only the three exemptions that are specifically set out in section 2 of the bill but also many other rights. In other words, this bill shall prevail only where it is not inconsistent with the Crowsnest rate structure, with the Maritime Freight Rates; Act, with the provisions in regard to compensation, or-and this is important-with a hundred other rights that may exist in a hundred other statutes. That is the intention of the amendment, and with all respect I must take exception to the point raised by the Prime Minister. I must take issue with his interpretation of the effect of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Provencher. The intention of the amendment is to safeguard rights that now exist under all statutes; it is intended that Bill No. 37 shall prevail only where it is not inconsistent with rights and functions that already exist with respect to employees or companies or corporations or citizens under the various acts now existent and which might be affected by the terms of this legislation.

speechtext:
I do not think there is
any doubt that that is the intention. The point of order I withdraw, but the effect of the amendment, if it ware adopted, would mean the abandonment of this bill. The bill is abandoned if the amendment is accepted.

speechtext: No, the whole thing falls.

As the clause
is drafted, it necessitates parliament legislating wholly in the dark, because it declares that, notwithstanding all statutes which may exist on any subject whatever, if their provisions conflict with any section of this bill, those particular provisions shall not be considered. Let me illustrate. There is a statute known as the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act which deals for instance, with matters of dispute between employees and the railway companies. If this section is permitted to remain as it is, and it suits the convenience of the person, whoever he may be, who is interpreting this statute to say that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act are inconsistent with its provisions, out that statute goes, and, I venture to say, without
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

any intention on the part of this House of Commons to bring about any such effect. What should be done is for this particular act to amend by its provisions existing acts in such a way that the effect of the amendment will be self-evident, we would then be enabled to see how far we are overriding the provisions of other acts. We should not; however, have a clause that goes the length of obliterating provisions of statutes passed for a variety of reasons and which undoubtedly, were they known, this house would wish to safeguard. To make my point clear, I shall ask the minister this question to which I venture to say he will not be able to reply: Will he tell us what particular statutes and what provisions in those statutes are there that may be inconsistent with this bill?

I should not like to
attempt to give a list of such statutes because I might omit some of them, but I will tell the right hon. gentleman that the statement he has made with reference to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is not correct because this would not affect it one particle. My right hon. friend is confusing inconsistent provisions with inconsistent statutes. He says that this would wipe out different statutes. It does mot propose to wipeout statutes but inconsistent provisions. May I, while agreeing with what the Prime Minister has said, point out also one most important respect in which this act would be made nugatory if the amendment moved by the hon. member for Provencher should carry. This legislation provides for cooperation and it provides for tribunals in cases of dispute. These provisions do not exist in the Railway Act and therefore the provisions in the Railway Act which are inconsistent with the provision in this act with respect to tribunals and also with respect to the bringing about of cooperation will be prevailed over by this act. The Railway Act is not prevailed over by this act except in so far as certain provisions of the former are inconsistent with this legislation, and that is the only effect this has. If however the amendment of the hon. member were to carry, it would indisputably have the effect of rendering the rest of this act null and void, because you would not then have tribunals as provided for in part III of this bill. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre sees the point. You could not have tribunals under this act at all if the hon. member's amendment carried, inasmuch as they would be inconsistent with the Railway Act and therefore that act would prevail and nullify this one. May I point out to the committee that this legislation has been 
considered by many lawyers in the Senate, and as the Prime Minister has pointed out it was deemed advisable after careful study that with respect to these three acts which are specified here, namely, section 176 of the Railway Act which deals with the matter of compensation in the case of moving a terminal; secondly, the Maritime Freight Rates Act; and, thirdly, the Crowsnest Pass legislation, they should be specifically set out by way of exemption.

It may be that, in the language of the Scotch, I am slow in the uptake, but as I read ,the first clause in section 2 I am still of the opinion that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Provencher is a direct negative. The clause as it is in the bill reads:
The provisions of this act. . . .shall prevail over all inconsistent provisions.
The hon. member wants this changed to read:
Shall prevail when not inconsistent.
If this act is to prevail only when the provisions of other acts are not inconsistent, it surely cannot prevail over inconsistent ones. The effect of the amendment therefore is virtually to say: "The provisions of this act shall bind His Majesty and shall not prevail over inconsistent provisions of other acts." Is that not simply to introduce a negative in front of the word "prevail"? The clause as it stands, reads, "shall prevail over all inconsistent provisions." The proposed amendment in fact reads, "shall not prevail over any inconsistent provision."
Is the hon. member speaking to a point of order?
Yes.
There is no point of order before the chair.

The statement was made that the amendment was not a negative. In my opinion it is a distinct negative. May I call attention to another difficulty that, it seems to me, exists arising out of the proposed amendment? The clause as it now reads is that this act shall prevail over all inconsistent provisions. In other words, it makes this an overriding act. I do not have to search other acts to find out inconsistent provisions;
I simply go to this act. Its provisions alone are relevant; the only relevant provisions of other acts are those that are inconsistent, and this measure provides that I do not need to bother my head about them. But if you insert the amendment which my hon. friend

C.N.R.-CP.R. Bill
is suggesting, what you are providing is this, that this act shall prevail only when the provisions of another act are not inconsistent. How, then, am I to know whether the provisions of this act are to prevail or not? I can ascertain that only by looking into all other acts to see whether there is in any of them any inconsistency with this act? I take this Railway Act and I cannot say whether upon a particular point it is the ruling, dominant act, because I am saddled with a condition which tells me that this provision may be of no use to me; that I must look at all the other acts to find out whether there may not be in them some inconsistency; and if I find some inconsistency in some other act, it overrules this. This will put a tremendous onus on people who are construing this legislation and will raise a great deal of difficulty concerning it; whereas as it now stands, it is quite simple. The clause makes this act rule, and you have not to consider anything but its provisions.

Those who drew up the original bill thought the words were advantageous for some reasons I do not know. When we studied the bill in this house, we considered the words unnecessary and after we had discussed the matter with those who drew up the original bill, they agreed. But as my hon. friend and my leader, who are lawyers, consider there is some doubt, and as these words are merely redundant, there is no objection to their remaining.
There is a certain amendment in regard to the word "or" which should have been placed in subsection 2 of the same section. Paragraph (a) of section 2 reads:
Any manufacturing, land, mining or ocean marine company, undertaking, property, work or service-
The word "or" should be inserted1 there, to make the bill more complete.
I move that.

Before section 2 passes the committee, I should like to say a few words in connection with it and to add another saving clause.
Is the hon. member now discussing section 2, subsection 1?

Yes. In my opinion this is a dangerous section. It may be designed to and it certainly will relieve unemployment among the members of the legal profession, because from now on we shall have plenty of work deciding what is consistent and what is not. I suppose as a lawyer I should be in accord with that part of the provision. It

C.N.R.-CP.R. Bill
seems to me, however, that we are going a long way when we enact legislation such as section 2, subsection 1, saying that this act shall prevail over all inconsistent provisions of all other acts. I am sorry at the attitude taken with respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Provencher. There come up in the house almost every year private bills in which special provisions are inserted that certain sections are to prevail so long as they are not inconsistent with, for instance, the Companies Act. The bill under consideration is in its nature a railway act, and in many private bills we have special provisions that the Railway Act, so far as it is not inconsistent with the bill at the time under discussion shall prevail. What the hon. member for Provencher is trying to do by his amendment, and what we are trying to do is to see that all this legislation which has been passed and has withstood the test of time shall not simply be wiped out by Bill A, No. 37, introduced by the Minister of Railways into this house. But now that we have been told that this thing is going through as it stands,
1	hope that I may have some better success than has been accorded to my hon. friends who have already moved amendments. I am hoping that mine may be one of those of which the minister was thinking when he said on the second reading that he would welcome amendments. I am hoping that my amendment to add to the saving clauses will be accepted. By the way, I am wondering just when those saving clauses came to the minds of those who framed this bill. I am told, for instance, that certainly paragraph (a) had not been thought of by the framers of this bill when it was introduced into the Senate, and I think I am on safe ground when I presume that pargraphs (b) and (c) had not been thought of when this bill was introduced. I think I am almost safe in saying that this bill when it was first drafted simply read, so far as section 2 is concerned:
The provisions of this act shall bind His Majesty and shall prevail over all inconsistent provisions of all other acts.
I think I am safe in that supposition. Then there came a doubt; there came pressure, "we must make certain". I commend my maritime friends for their insistence on matters of this kind. They' have made certain that the Maritime Freight Rates Act will not be made inconsistent with the provisions of this act, and that there shall be exports through Canadian ports, as is provided by subsection
2	of section 14. Someone else suggested that we must make sure that the members of the various railway organizations be protected. And so in a great gesture paragraph (a) was

inserted as a saving clause. I wonder if hon. members know how far that paragraph (a) does go in the protection of railway employees in the light of further provisions of this act and in the light of what we know is happening and will happen in respect to the laying off of railway men in this country. Paragraph (a) refers to section 179 of the Railway Act. which is chapter 170 of the revised statutes of 1927, which provides for compensation. Section 179 of the Railway Act provides that where there is a change,
The company shall compensate its employees as the board-
Meaning the Board of Railway Commissioners.
-deems proper for any financial loss caused to them by change of residence-
Change of residence only.
-necessitated thereby.
Suppose terminals are closed and men are dismissed, as I submit they are going to be wholesale, then section 179 of the Railway Act and this saving clause (a), which hon. gentlemen opposite boast of having put in. is absolutely worthless to the employees of the Canadian National Railways.
If we are going to start putting in saving clauses, let us stop right here at section 2 until we have gone through all the various acts which have been passed and which have withstood the test of time, and see whether any of their provisions are inconsistent with the provisions of this bill. The minister says: I cannot tell you how many such there are. That is going to be a very interesting question. Let us pause before we legislate in this house for the future by a bill as drastic as this. In order to show the absurdity of having a provision of this kind, having simply saving clauses (a), (b) and (c) and not going on and inserting saving clauses (d), (e) and (f), and so on, I am going to move an amendment to add one other saving clause. I could add a dozen, but I am going to move to add only one simply to show what the minister is getting into and what we may expect for the future of this bill. The amendment I am going to move is with respect to section 23 of the present Canadian. National Railways Act, which I say is entirely inconsistent with the powers given to the trustees under this bill. I say now, as I said on the second reading, that under this bill the trustees are permitted to allow lines to be abandoned without any regard to parliament, without any regard to the Board of Railway Commissioners, without any regard to the governor in council. If the bill means anything, certainly that is what it is intended to mean. It was to give

the board of trustees this power without any regard to the Board of Railway Commissioners or tihe governor in council or parliament.
Let me read section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act, not the Railway Act to which the minister referred a few moments ago in speaking to one horn, member. The Railway Act proper is chapter 170 of the statutes of 1927, but the Canadian National Railways Act, as the minister well knows, is a special act that was passed in 1920, at which time the Canadian National as we know it was created. It deals with the appointment of directors, the powers of directors, and matters of that kind. Section 23 of that act, being chapter 172 of the statutes of 1927, has this marginal note: "Power to abandon line, and dismantle or dispose thereof by consent," and reads as follows:
23. With the approval of the governor in council, and upon the recommendation of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the company may abandon the operation of any lines-
I draw attention to that, that it must be with the approval of the governor in council:
-or parts of lines of railway and incidental works, the operation or continued maintenance whereof has, in the opinion of the Board of Railway Commissioners, become unnecessary or inexpedient through duplication-
That is exactly what we find to-day, and the minister has pointed out, and in many cases rightly so, that these duplications make for certain abandonments, which is quite true:
[DOT]-or other economical considerations;
The very tenor of this bill.
-and with the consent of a majority in value of the registered security holders affected may dismantle or dispose of the lines of railway or works so abandoned.
I think I should also read subsection 2 of section 23, in order that it may be a matter of record. It deals with the consent of the security holders for such abandonment, and reads, the consent having been referred to just prior to that in subsection 1 of section 23:
Such consent may be given by a majority ini value of the registered security holders present ait any meeting, in person or by proxy, called by the president of the company, to be held at any time or place stated by him, on notice in writing sent by registered mail to all of the registered security holders at least one calendar month before the date of the meeting; or may be given by a majority in value of the registered security holders by written consents filed with the company upon a circular stating the facts being sent by registered mail to all of the registered security holders.
It is interesting to note that when this section was discussed in the house at the time the original Canadian National Railways Act was considered in the House of Commons in
1919-many hon. members, including the minister himself, were in the house at that time 

the gentleman piloting the bill through the House of Commons, now the leader of the government in another place, them acting Minister of Justice, had this to say with respect to section 23. Someone had raised the point with respect to the security holders, and the whole debate turned on many of the subject matters that we are now considering, namely, the control by parliament over matters dealt with in the legislation that was then being considered-and by the way the government had eventually to put closure, on in order to pass that particular bill. It had been suggested to Mr. Meighen, then Acting Minister of Justice, that clause 23 was a far-reaching clause, and he replied, as reported in Hansard of 1919, volume 2, page 1709:
In so far as the security holders are concerned, their consent is obtained, but their security is not lost. This would only be a small part of their security that would be dismantled and abandoned, and they would see the wisdom of adopting that course and would consent accordingly. Inasmuch as the whole idea of this measure is the joining together for operating purposes of lines that were formerly under several managements, there will presumably be cases of duplication that may be cut out without injury to the public, and the intention of this section is to provide that that may be done.
Then, let me call the attention of the minister to this part of Mr. Meighen's speech;
The Board of Railway Commissioners is entrusted from the point of view of public convenience and safety with deciding what is necessary and what is not in the way of service. Consequently that is the tribunal, it seems to me, to which resort should be had to determine whether any small part or branch is a duplication or for other reasons may be abandoned.
Those are the words of the right hon. gentleman who introduced and piloted this present bill through the Senate only a few weeks ago. I submit that we should hesitate before we place in the hands of trustees, I care not who they may be, this power which up to the present has been exercised only after careful consideration by the Board of Railway Commissioners, with the governor in council as the final body to whom appeal may be taken from a decision of the board, we should hesitate before we take out of the hands of these men control of abandonments which would be to the detriment not only of eastern Canada but of western Canada as well, where lines have been built, and around which community centres have grown up. If, as the Prime Minister has said, this is a saving clause, then let us add another to (a), (b) and (c) which will save the rights of these branch lines and community centres, and
CJV.R.-CR.R. Bill

which will protect those who have gone into new communities, and not place them at the mercy of trustees who think only of dollars and cents and not of the welfare of the community as a whole. With that in mind I beg to move the following amendment to the bill:
That section 2, subsection 1, be amended by adding thereto a clause to be lettered (d) "and the provisions of section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act, 1920."

The hon. member has elaborated the point of his amendment, but I should like him in a few words to state his meaning. I do not suggest that he has confused the issue, but I should like to have explained to me the object of the amendment he has proposed.

I am glad the minister is not the judge before whom I sometimes appear, because if he were I am afraid I would not win many cases. I am attempting to show to the minister that I want to preserve what is contained in. section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act, so that the board of trustees to whom he is giving all these powers shall not be able to go out and abandon lines, considering only the dollars and cents, without there being someone to whom we as members of parliament and, if you like, shareholders of the Canadian National Railways can go. Under section 23 the abandonment of a line must first have the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and then on the recommendation of the board the governor in council are for the time being directors acting on behalf of the people-I care not what you call them-the cabinet of this country. Those directors come into their places and we the shareholders can rise in our places and condemn or approve the abandonment of those lines. I know the minister will be fair in the matter, and I plead with him not to pass this section until he provides for that safety with respect to the abandonment of lines.

Mr. Chairman, to deal
instantly with an amendment such as the hon. member has just moved, and apparently to which he has given considerable thought, is difficult. However, may I offer one or two suggestions to him? In the first place, so far as section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act is concerned-and I am giving my interpretation only as a layman, because as he knows I am not a lawyer-the section will remain to a large extent in force, with the exception that the trustees will act in the place of the directors. So far as the abandonment of lines is concerned I have this to say: Suppose under the present bill the Canadian 
National wished to abandon some portion of its territory, irrespective of the possibility of any cooperative measures, the trustees would still have to come before the Board of Railway Commissioners and obtain consent. But suppose it were dealing with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the change was being made for cooperative purposes, if there was any objection made by either of the companies an arbitral tribunal would1 be set up. Even then the arbitral tribunal would not have the power to carry out a cooperative measure unless the chairman of that tribunal agreed with the measure. And hon. members must bear in mind that the chairman of the arbitral tribunal is the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

I do not wish to interrupt
the minister's line of thought, but may I point out to him that in addition to the powers given to the directors as outlined in the Railway Act, he must take note of subsection 6 of section 9 of the bill, which reads that:
(6) No order, regulation, by-law, act, decision or proceeding of the trustees shall require the approval of His Majesty-
And I presume His Majesty in this instance means the governor in council, if it means anything. Certainly it must mean parliament, but let us assume for the sake of argument that it means governor in council. Let me proceed with subsection 6:
-or that of any other shareholder of any company to which this section applies.
The section referred to is that which transfers to these trustees the powers of the directors of the Canadian National Railways as they obtain under the Canadian National Railways Act.

I agree
with the hon. member who has just spoken, and I am sorry I cannot follow the argument of the minister in connection with the bill. He said the trustees will still have to go before the Board of Railway Commissioners in regard to the abandonment of branch lines. I cannot find provision for such procedure.
I refer to the abandonment of services. The directors have to go to the board at the present time.
Yes, but they are being abolished'. You are appointing a board of trustees.

Under the Railway Act
the board of trustees would not be able to abandon services to any greater extent than they are abandoned at the present time.

But there is no safeguard ini this legislation. That is what the hon. member is stating, and' that is the condition we wish to guard against in the amendment submitted. I think the minister confuses the trustees with the arbitral tribunal. The arbitral tribunal has nothing to do with the point raised by the hon. member for West Lamlbton. They come into play only when there is a dispute between the two railway systems. In this legislation the government is seeking to appoint what may be known as an arbitral board of trustees. They are given sweeping powers whereby they are not subject to the approval of the governor in council. They could abandon branch lines without going before the Board of Railway Commissioners, without going before the governor in council or before this parliament.

The hon. member referred to subsection (6) of section 9. I call to his attention the fact that in subsection 2 of section 9 page 6 of the bill we find the following:
The trustees shall and may thereafter, subject to the provisions of this act, have and exercise all the powers, rights, privileges and immunities, and perform and be subject to all the duties, responsibilities and restrictions, which now appertain to the board of directors of the national company.

Mr. Chairman, if the minister
will agree here and now to the deletion of subsection 6 of section 9 I might consider the withdrawal of my amendment.

I believe we should deal
with subsection 6 of section 9 when we come to it.

I did not raise the question
with regard to that section.

Yes, my hon. friend did
raise it a moment ago. We should deal with subsection 6 of section 9 when we come to it, not under section 2.

The
point applies equally to the minister, who has just dealt with subsection 2 of section 9. May I reread part of it:
The trustees shall and may thereafter, subject to the provisions of this act, have and exercise all the powers, rights, privileges and immunities. . . .
These are new powers which the directors never had under the Canadian National Railways Act. You are giving them powers apart from the governor in council, apart from parliament, and without any limit whatever. Subsection 2 is subject only to the provisions of this act. There is no comparison whatever between the powers of the trustees under this act and the powers of the directors under the old Canadian National Railways Act.

I think my hon. friend
should read all of it, not merely part of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I say a word, Mr. Chairman? I do not desire to trespass upon the time of the committee, but I am amazed at some observations that have been made. That, of course, may be because I have been unable to grasp the situation as it has been presented. Section 9 provides that-
When the governor in council shall proclaim in the Canada Gazette that he has vacated all nominations to the board of directors of the national company and has appointed trustees as by section 4 of this act provided the said board shall^ cease to exist-
That eliminates the board.
-'and, by force of this act and without more, the direction and control of the national company and its undertaking shall be vested, subject to the provisions of this act, in the trustees.
That is the substitution of the trustees for the directors. Then follow the subsections to which attention has been directed, by which it is perfectly clear that the trustees are clothed with wide powers additional to those they may exercise by virtue of succeeding the former board of directors. But will the committee be good enough to look at subsection 4 of the Caandian National Railways Act? It says:
(4) The National Act and all statutes, charters, letters patent and orders in council of Canada which relate to any of such companies in Canada shall, in so far as they may be inconsistent with the provisions of this section, be read in the light hereof and be construed so as to conform herewith.
That is right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That makes it perfectly clear that the Canadian National Railways Act, so far as it is possible to read that act with this, muS be read to conform with the provisions of this measure, letter A of the Senate, Bill No. 37. If the hon. gentleman will examine with a little more care the provision at the top of page 7 of the bill, subsection 6, of section 9, having given evidence of his astuteness as a lawyer he will realize that that subsection does not deal with orders in council, has nothing to do with orders in council. The shareholder of all the national railways is His Majesty, in the right of the dominion, and he is registered as such. It will be observed that inasmuch as you have to appeal to ithe shareholders under the pro-
C.N.R.-CP.R. Bill

visions of some statutes, and inasmuch as His Majesty is a shareholder, when it says-
No order, regulation, by-law, act, decision or proceeding of the trustees shall require the approval of His Majesty or that of any other shareholder of any company to which this section applies.
-that means His Majesty qua shareholder- not the governor in council, not the cabinet, not anything else except His Majesty as a shareholder. The crown is the shareholder of the Canadian National at the present moment, and it shall not apply to His Majesty or to any other shareholder, that is the half dozen people who have been selected for the purpose of constituting quorums and matters of that kind. That is the reason that provision wias put there. I think the hon. member for West Lamb ton will remember the rule of law, ejusdem generis. Here you have the words, "H>is Majesty or any other shareholder," the words "His Majesty" mean His Majesty as a shareholder or any other shareholder. Under the general rule affecting railways as provided by the Railway Act and other statutes you have to call a meeting of shareholders to deal with certain matters that the directors have set in motion, their power being to set the machinery in motion. This subsection merely provides that no appeal is necessary to the .shareholders. Neither the consent of the crown in the right of His Majesty is required, nor that of the other shareholders of the company. That is all it means. As I read section 23, to which the hon. gentleman has referred, there is nothing in the bill inconsistent with this section. As far as I am concerned at the present moment, without looking at it in more detail, section 23 is unaffected by this legislation. It has not yet been pointed out in what sense it is affected. Just let us look at it:
With the approval of the governor in council, and upon the recommendation of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the company may abandon the operation of any lines or parts of lines of railway and incidental works, the operation or continued maintenance whereof has, in the opinion of the Board of Railway Commissioners, become unnecessary or inexpedient through duplication, or other economical eonsiderati ons;-
As I see it at the moment there is no inconsistency between the two; this section in its force and vigour is retained. Nothing that has been said this evening, no reference that has been made to the statute affords a reason for changing that view. The supreme purpose of the statute is not to take from the security holders any powers they possess or any rights they enjoy, but rather to say, as this act has said, that unless they consent

to action being taken the action cannot be taken. After all, as I said the other day, although an endeavour was made by many people to have it misunderstood, the equity of redemption in these roads is all that we have, and inasmuch as they were built without a single dollar of capital being put up other than that represented by the securities, the non-payment of interest on the securities put them in the defaulting class had it not been for the guarantee given by the Dominion of Canada. That guarantee is what saves them from receivership, and the trustees in this case are merely trying to preserve the rights of the security holders who really built the roads in question on the bonds guaranteed by the dominion. There never was, although it was hoped there would be, any value in the equity of redemption; there is none now. As far as this section of the statute is concerned I see nothing at the moment that would induce me to believe, unless I hear arguments more powerful than I have yet heard,-and I do not reflect on the power of the arguments made-that there is any inconsistency between that provision and section 23.

If . that were the effect of this provision there would be no trouble at all so far as the amendment is concerned, and if the right hon. gentleman will accept the spirit of the amendment of the hon. member for West Lambton I think all on this side will be satisfied. The Prime Minister cited subsection 4, which exactly proves the contention of the hon. member for West Lambton. The Canadian National Railways Act, and all statutes, and so forth, which relate to any such companies, shall, in so far as they may be inconsistent with the provisions of this section, be read in the light hereof and be construed so as to conform herewith. What does that mean? It means where there is any inconsistency between the Canadian National Railways Act and Bill No. 37, the Canadian National Railways Act must be subsidiary to the provisions of this bill.

The hon. gentleman has just made one mistake. If he will look at subsection 4, he will observe that the inconsistency must be "with the provisions of this section," and that is the section which substitutes the trustees for the directors. I am sorry the hon. gentleman should think that the inconsistency must be with the act; it deals only with the trustees, and the substitution of them for the directors. Any inconsistency between the Canadian National Railways Act and this-and there are many-must be read in the light of this section.

Section
9 gives the trustees certain powers. In the first place, it abolishes the directors and, in the second place it constitutes the trustees. The powers of the trustees are practically set out in this section 9.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
look at section 3?

I have
read that. I am now referring to the subsection which the Prime Minister read, subsection 4. There may be inconsistencies with the provisions of the section which confers the powers upon the board of trustees which is to take the place of the board of directors created by the Canadian National act. Let us now consider subsection 6, also referred to by the Prime Minister. This reads:
No order, regulation, by-law, act, decision or proceeding of the trustees shall require the approval of His Majesty or that of any other shareholder of any company to which this section applies.
It is not material whether this refers to His Majesty in the capacity of a shareholder or in any other capacity, the effect of the subsection is that His Majesty has no control over any order, any regulation, any by-law, any act, any decision or any proceeding of the trustees which is being set up under section 9. That is the fundamental and vital difference between this bill and the Canadian National act. A board of trustees is being substituted for the old board of directors and the trustees are given powers which the directors never had. The directors were always subject to the governor in council and there is not a single clause in this bill which subjects the board of trustees to the dictates of the governor in council. Their acts cannot be discussed even by parliament. There is no comparison between the powers granted to the trustees under section 9 and the powers granted to the board of directors under the Canadian National act. Subsection 4 of section 9 specifically states that where the provisions of the Canadian National act are inconsistent with the provisions of this section, then the provisions of the act shall be of no avail. It is intended that this bill shall override the provisions of the Canadian National act. That has been our fight all along. As I stated on the second reading of the bill, it means the abandonment of government control and government ownership of the Canadian National railways.

I should like to add a word or two to the argument of my hon. friend from Vancouver. If the argument made by the Prime Minister is sound, surely he would have no objection to stating in the bill that
section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act shall not be deemed to be inconsistent with the provisions of this bill or to be in any way affected thereby. There seems to be some dispute between those who believe they are capable of interpreting the meaning of this bill, and its provisions should be made dear. Apparently a similar dispute arose in the other house in connection with the provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and in order to make it quite clear subsections (a), (b) and (c) were inserted. As I understand it, there is no difference between hon. members on either side of the house in .connection with the principle that before any branch line or section of road shall be torn up someone other than the trustees whom we have set up shall pass upon the action, that the human element shall be taken into some consideration and that responsibility shall be placed upon the shoulders of someone other than this irresponsible board of trustees. I submit that this matter could be easily settled by the government accepting the amendment of the hon. member for West Lambton.

In connection with section 23 of the National act, I still adhere to the position that where the trustees decide upon the abandonment of any branch line or service, they would have to appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners just the same as the directors must appeal.
Where is that?

The Railway Act still
applies except those sections which are inconsistent. That section is not inconsistent. Another point which I should like to bring out is that if section 23 were put into the present bill as proposed by the hon. member for West Lambton, the arbitral tribunals would be rendered useless. There will be times when an arbitral tribunal will meet for the purpose of deciding whether a branch line shall be abandoned or a joint service inaugurated.
I am hopeful that the tribunal will be the Board of Railway Commissioners.

That is another matter.
I take the position that section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act, while perhaps not completely, will be to a large extent still in operation even after this bill goes into effect. I differ from my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre. If that section were included in this bill it might and I think it would interfere with the power of the tribunals in dealing with cooperative abandonment of certain branch lines or the decision to operate

a joint service or something of that sort. I do not think the amendment of the hon. member for West Lambton should be accepted.

It has been intimated that we are agreed on both sides of the house that no branch lines shall be scrapped without the trustees having to appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners. If the minister accepts that view, surely we could agree upon some clause which would make it absolutely clear.

Apparently the Prime Minister and the Minister' of Railways are not in agreement as to the effect of this amendment. The Prime Minister has stated that there is sufficient provision in this bill to safeguard what my hon. friend wants to obtain by his amendment. The Minister of Railways tells the committee that he is afraid of the effect of including a safeguarding clause in the bill which would retain the provisions of section 23 of the Canadian National act. The minister is afraid that such a section would disturb the functions of that august and majestic arbitral tribunal. I suggest that there is nothing in the amendment which would hinder the work of the arbitral tribunal; it would mean that the consent of the governor in council would have to be obtained to whatever was proposed by the private and national systems in connection with the abandonment of lines. We want to safeguard against the wholesale slaughter of branch lines throughout Canada without parliament having a single word to say. I repeat what I said before:	This is a final abdication of the principle of democratic control and ownership of the Canadian National system. The Prime Minister says we are not losing that and the Minister of Railways says we are. The minister has stated that if this amendment is added to the bill it will interfere with the work of the tribunal. The Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways might agree among themselves that the abandonment of a branch line would be in the interests of economy. Cooperation by direction is covered by part II of the bill, and cooperation by compulsion is made possible by part III. I ask the minister to show me one clause or one sentence in this bill which will give us the right asked for by the hon. member for West Lambton, that section 23 shall be preserved for the people of Canada in the legislation we are now considering.

I do not know offhand [DOT]
that I can show my hon. friend the section,

but I still maintain that the trustees are in exactly 'the same position with regard to the abandonment of lines as are 'the directors under the legislation which exists at the moment. Dealing only with section- 23 of the Canadian National act, I say that the trustees will be in exactly the same position in having to go 'before the board as the directors are now. That is my claim.

Will the minister show me where that appears in the act? I understood him to say that the trustees were in the same position as the directors of the Canadian National Railways in regard to obtaining the consent of the governor in council-
I did not say that.

I understood him to say that the board of trustees under this legislation was in exactly the same position as the directors of the Canadian National Railways under the Canadian National Act and I submit that that -is not so. Even though 'the minister may find some section here which I cannot find, which might make it desirable for the trustees to go before the Board of Railway Commissioners, there is nothing in this legislation that makes it necessary for them to obtain the consent of the governor in council in regard to the abandonment of a single branch line.

I am informed by the
legal advisers that there is nothing in this act that takes away reference to the governor in council so far as the trustees are concerned.

Then
will the minister agree to the representations made on this side of the house to have a specific clause inserted that will maintain the right of endorsation. by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There should be certain fundamental principles to apply to the case. First, if I followed the hon. gentleman fairly, and I think I did, let me ask: Where in this bill do you find any section that provides that section 23 of the Canadian National Railway * Act does not apply?

In what the Prime Minister has said this evening with regard to subsection 6 of section 9, he gives an entirely different interpretation of the measure from that which all of us on this side of the house had given it up to the time he spoke. If he wishes to be understood in the light of what he has just said, I will say at once that many of the objections which we have to the measure are removed; we want, however to have the point made perfectly clear. As

Official Report of Debates
we have understood the subsection up to the present time, we have taken it to mean that all provisions in the former act, which require consent on the part of the governor in council to certain actions by the trustees, were being wholly removed, and that no order, regulation, by-law, act, decision or proceeding of the trustees shall require the approval of His Majesty. We were reading that in absolute terms as referring to all acts-any act of the trustees. As I now understand it the Prime Minister interprets the section as follows: No order, regulation, by-law, act, decision or proceeding of the trustees, in so far as it relates to this section and this section only, shall require the approval of His Majesty or that of any other shareholder of any company to which this section applies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not what I said. I desired to convey to the committee this meaning: that His Majesty, here, was referred to as a shareholder-"or that of any other shareholder''-and that the rule ejusdem generis applies, namely, that where you have the words "His Majesty" they must mean His Majesty as a shareholder, because that is clearly what is meant. All our legislation is based on the assumption that the shareholders must express their approval. For instance, in the Canadian National Railways Act there is a list of several pages of companies-a page and a half-to which it applies; and under the general law, whenever certain acts or bylaws have to be made effective, the shareholders must be called together to give approval. Now, we have provided in subsection 6 that no order, regulation, by-law, act, decision or proceeding of the trustees shall require the approval of His Majesty or that of any other shareholder of any company to which this section applies.
